title: Teresa's reform
hook: Teresa founds small, poor, joyful convents on dusty roads
tomorrow: John of the Cross in prison

segments.voice: Yesterday, Xavier to Asia, dying within sight of China. Your line was to the ends of the earth. Who far away did you reach, by distance or by difference? Day eight hundred seventy-five.

The convent had a parlor, and the parlor was busy. Friends dropped by. Relatives brought news. Nuns from good families kept their comforts, and talked through the grille with visitors for hours. One of those nuns, in the Spanish city of Ávila, was witty, warm, and very good company, and she enjoyed the parlor as much as anyone. She later wrote that, for a long stretch of her life, her prayer was half-hearted, pulled between God and the world. Then something in her turned, and she began to want something much smaller and much simpler. Her name was Teresa. Today: Teresa's reform.

Teresa's idea was simple. A small house. Only a handful of sisters. Poor, living on what was given. Enclosed, so the parlor wouldn't run the day. Simple habits, and sandals instead of shoes, which is why her nuns came to be called discalced, meaning unshod. Time for silent prayer every day. And joy: she wanted her sisters cheerful, not grim. Her first small house in Ávila met fierce opposition from the town and from her own order. She opened it anyway. Then she went out on the roads of Spain, in rough covered carts, through heat and dust and mud, founding more houses. There's a story people tell from those journeys. Thrown from a cart into a muddy river, she complained to God, and heard that this is how he treats his friends. Her answer: no wonder you have so few. Whether or not it happened, it sounds like her. Teresa wasn't only an organizer. She wrote about prayer as a journey inward through a castle of many rooms, with God at the center. And among her papers, tradition says, was found a short poem. In English it goes something like this: let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you; all things are passing, God does not change; patience gains everything; whoever has God lacks nothing; God alone is enough. It sounds like what Jesus told a busy Martha, in the King James Bible: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful." The Catholic Church names Teresa a saint and a Doctor of the Church. She is a reformer who made things smaller, so there would be room for the one thing.

Here's the practice: simplify one routine. Settle, and breathe. Pick one ordinary routine: your morning, your phone before bed, the way you leave the house, the way you start work. Walk through it slowly in your mind. Notice the steps that crowd it. Then imagine doing it with one thing fewer, the way Teresa cut a convent down to its center. Don't fix it yet. Just see it. If you pray, you can say her line slowly: let nothing disturb you. If you don't, just let it be quiet for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Teresa's reform. Small, poor, joyful houses of prayer that Teresa of Ávila founded along the roads of Spain, cutting convent life down to its center.

Your line: let nothing disturb you. This week ran from Cranmer's hand and Thomas More, through burnings on both sides, Trent, Ignatius and Xavier, to Teresa. Today, take one thing out of one routine, and keep it out. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Discalced Carmelite nuns still live in small enclosed communities shaped by Teresa's reform, and her short poem beginning "let nothing disturb you" is prayed and sung by Catholics and others, often as a short repeated chant.

fork.setup: you're Teresa, a well-liked nun in a large, comfortable convent with a busy parlor. you want more room for prayer. what do you do?
options: stay, and pray harder in the busy house.
found a small, poor house with a handful of sisters.
fork.reveal: she founds a small, poor house in Ávila over fierce opposition, then takes to the roads to found more.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nun who made convent life stricter.
what it means: a reformer who made things smaller and simpler, so prayer and joy had room.
what a scholar hears: discalced means unshod; her houses took the name from their sandals, and her short poem, nada te turbe, was found among her papers.
recall: a name their opponents gave them
